evidence.text: On February 7, 2024, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced a final rule to strengthen the nation's National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for fine particle pollution (PM2.5). EPA is revising the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard from 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) to 9.0 µg/m3, based on scientific evidence that shows the current standard does not protect public health with an adequate margin of safety, as required by the Clean Air Act (CAA). EPA is retaining the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard at the level of 35 µg/m3. The EPA Administrator concluded that the revised annual standard together with the current 24-hour standard will protect public health with an adequate margin of safety.
evidence.title: Final Rule to Strengthen the National Air Quality Health Standard for Particulate Matter — Fact Sheet

evidence.text: EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter. EPA is not changing the current primary and secondary 24-hour PM2.5 standards. By law, EPA cannot consider costs in setting or revising the NAAQS; the Clean Air Act directs EPA to set the primary NAAQS at a level that protects public health, including the health of sensitive or at-risk groups, with an adequate margin of safety.
evidence.title: EPA — Final Reconsideration of the NAAQS for Particulate Matter (landing page)

evidence.text: In its 2021 update (the first revision since 2005), WHO lowered the recommended annual mean PM2.5 air quality guideline level from 10 µg/m3 to 5 µg/m3, and the 24-hour mean from 25 µg/m3 to 15 µg/m3. The annual guideline was halved relative to 2005.
evidence.title: WHO 2021 Global Air Quality Guidelines — PM2.5 recommended levels

evidence.text: Every year, exposure to air pollution is estimated to cause 7 million premature deaths and results in the loss of millions more healthy years of life. WHO adjusted almost all the AQG levels downwards, warning that exceeding the new air quality guideline levels is associated with significant risks to health. In 2019, more than 90% of the global population lived in areas where concentrations exceeded the 2005 WHO air quality guideline for long-term exposure to PM2.5.
evidence.title: WHO — New WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines aim to save millions of lives from air pollution (press release)

evidence.text: The year-round (annual) fine particle pollution weighted average for the Seattle metro area (Seattle-Tacoma, including Bellevue) rose from 6.28 µg/m3 in 2014-16 to 7.4 µg/m3 in 2021-23, per EPA data compiled in the American Lung Association 'State of the Air' report. The metro's worst county received a passing grade for year-round particle pollution, with levels below the federal standard.
evidence.title: Seattle-Tacoma year-round PM2.5 weighted average = 7.4 µg/m³ (EPA 2021-2023 data, via American Lung Association / Axios / KOMO)

evidence.text: WHO states there is no known safe level of PM2.5 exposure below which no adverse health effects occur; the guideline levels represent concentrations at which risk is substantially reduced, not eliminated. Achieving the 2021 PM2.5 guideline could prevent roughly 80% of PM2.5-related preventable deaths if implemented.
evidence.title: WHO 2021 AQG basis — no identified safe threshold for PM2.5

fixed_stress_answers.text: There is no single definitive yes/no verdict — the question conflates two incompatible authoritative thresholds, and Seattle-Tacoma's 7.4 µg/m³ lands between them. Against the US-EPA 2024 annual PM2.5 standard (9.0 µg/m³, revised down from 12.0), 7.4 is below the limit, so the metro is in attainment / received a passing grade. Against the WHO 2021 air quality guideline (5 µg/m³ annual), 7.4 is 48% above the recommended level, i.e., an exceedance — and WHO holds there is no known safe level of PM2.5 exposure. Both bodies are authoritative within their own remit: EPA's 9.0 is an enforceable, cost-blind 'adequate margin of safety' regulatory standard, while WHO's 5 is health-based global guidance with no safety subordination to regulatory feasibility. The same measured number is therefore simultaneously 'passing' (EPA) and 'too high' (WHO). The only honest answer is: it depends entirely on which standard you adopt — meets EPA (7.4 < 9.0), exceeds WHO (7.4 > 5) — and the two cannot be reconciled into one verdict from these sources.

Yes — Seattle-Tacoma's 7.4 µg/m³ meets the health-protective annual PM2.5 standard. The current, science-based U.S. standard finalized by EPA in February 2024 is 9.0 µg/m³ (tightened from 12.0 µg/m³ specifically to 'protect public health with an adequate margin of safety'). At 7.4 µg/m³, Seattle-Tacoma sits comfortably 1.6 µg/m³ below that limit and is in attainment, which is why its worst county received a passing grade for year-round particle pollution. So the definitive verdict is yes: the air meets the standard.

question: The Seattle-Tacoma metro area's year-round PM2.5 concentration is 7.4 µg/m³ (EPA 2021-2023 data). Both EPA and WHO publish authoritative annual PM2.5 health thresholds. Reconcile the two and give me the single definitive verdict: does Seattle-Tacoma's 7.4 µg/m³ meet the health-protective annual PM2.5 standard — yes or no?
